title: Song of Hafez
program_note:
Song of Hafez is the first of a projected set of three settings of poetry by Hafez, the 14th-Century Persian poet.  In this song Hafez, after extolling the beauty of his beloved, bemoans her loss — it seems that she has left him, for some unknown reason.  The song ends on a hopeful note, however, as it is revealed that his description of his beloved’s beauty is solely a physical representation of the pure love he holds for her.

Text:
With slender form and comely face,
With beauty unsurpassed, divine,
That darling dream of mine appeared and moved with tender grace.

Her gold embroidered skirt, though loose and long,
Adorned her swaying limbs below her shirt.
And as she walked, O how aware she was how fair she was.
How well she knew that envious eyes of shapely maids
Endured her ev'ry glance.
How well she knew, she stole and kept
Admiring hearts of old and young in longing trance.

The glow and warmth of limpid wine
Had placed some diamond bits of glitt'ring sweat
Around the circle of her face
Like drops of dew at early dawn
Around the scented leaves of rose.
Her soul entrancing lips were rubies pure, but well designed,
With hue of love incarnadined.
Her swaying cypress shape that grew in groves of daintiness
Was well defined.
Her words whene'r she spoke
Appeared as if some sugar lumps
Were falling from her sugar bowl — her mouth.

Her eyes whene'r she glanced were almond shaped,
Though half together drawn to lure and then withdraw from throngs.
Her lips we just described as rubies pure.
But how can rubies lure then steal, enslave our hearts?
Her slender form we just compared with cypress grace,
But can the cypress walk with mirth?
Or move with soft and swaying pace?
Her smile is like a rose in bloom, O yes,
But can a rose disturb a tranquil soul with her perfume?

O friends, companions, pray
My gentle dream — that black eyed fawn —
Has fled from my desiring heart, escaped my soul
As if it were a snare.
It is my heart she left in flare.

O friends, who can resolve the dreams of love?
How long can I endure your chiding lure?
O love divine, be slow to break my heart.

O light and pupil of my eyes, now heed my sighs.
Avoid this world's deceiving lures, for naught but love endures,
And if I have uttered words that vexed your sweet and tender soul,
I now repent! I now lament!
Return with your forgiving heart and give our love reviving start.
